payload.stem: Two carts of equal mass $0.5\text{ kg}$ at rest on a frictionless track are pushed apart by a compressed spring between them. The spring releases a total of $6\text{ J}$ of energy, which becomes kinetic energy of the carts, and the carts have equal kinetic energy because their masses are equal: $3.00\text{ J}$ each. In a second trial one of the carts is replaced by a cart with $2$ times the mass, and the spring releases the same $6\text{ J}$. What is the best prediction of the kinetic energy of the lighter cart in the second trial?

options.why: Gives all of the energy to the lighter cart.
Momentum is conserved, so $mv_1=(2m)v_2$ and $v_1=2v_2$. The kinetic energies are in the ratio $K_1:K_2=2:1$, so the lighter cart has the fraction $2/(2+1)$ of $6\text{ J}$, which is $4.00\text{ J}$.
Gives the lighter cart the inverse share, $E/(1+f)$.
Gives the lighter cart the same share as before, ignoring the larger mass of the other cart.

payload.stem: In a hydraulic lift a small piston of area $2\text{ cm}^2$ is pushed down with a force of $20\text{ N}$ through a distance of $0.3\text{ m}$. The incompressible fluid transmits the pressure to a large piston of area $20\text{ cm}^2$. Friction is negligible. Which statement about the work done on the small piston and by the fluid on the large piston is correct and best justified?

options.text: The work done on the large piston is less than the work done on the small piston, because the fluid loses energy transmitting the force.
options.why: Assumes that energy is lost in the fluid even though friction is negligible and the fluid is incompressible.

options.text: The work done on the large piston is $10$ times as great, because the force on it is $10$ times as great.
options.why: Multiplies the work by the force factor without noticing that the large piston moves a proportionally smaller distance.

options.text: The work done on the small piston is $10$ times as great, because the small piston must be pushed with more pressure.
options.why: Confuses the pressure in the fluid with the force; the pressure is the same on both pistons.

options.text: The work is the same for both pistons, $6.00\text{ J}$, because the large piston gets a force $10$ times as great but moves only $1/10$ of the distance, so the force and distance changes cancel.
options.why: The pressure is equal, so $F_2=200\text{ N}$; the fluid volume is conserved, so $d_2=d_1/10=0.0300\text{ m}$; then $W_2=F_2d_2=6.00\text{ J}=W_1$.

payload.stem: Two carts of equal mass $0.5\text{ kg}$ at rest on a frictionless track are pushed apart by a compressed spring between them. The spring releases a total of $4\text{ J}$ of energy, which becomes kinetic energy of the carts, and the carts have equal kinetic energy because their masses are equal: $2.00\text{ J}$ each. In a second trial one of the carts is replaced by a cart with $4$ times the mass, and the spring releases the same $4\text{ J}$. What is the best prediction of the kinetic energy of the lighter cart in the second trial?

options.why: Gives the lighter cart the inverse share, $E/(1+f)$.
Gives all of the energy to the lighter cart.
Gives the lighter cart the same share as before, ignoring the larger mass of the other cart.
Momentum is conserved, so $mv_1=(4m)v_2$ and $v_1=4v_2$. The kinetic energies are in the ratio $K_1:K_2=4:1$, so the lighter cart has the fraction $4/(4+1)$ of $4\text{ J}$, which is $3.20\text{ J}$.

payload.stem: A solid sphere and a solid disk, each of mass $4\text{ kg}$ and radius $0.2\text{ m}$, are mounted on identical frictionless axles through their centers and start from rest. options.text: The solid sphere is spinning faster ($187\text{ rad/s}$ compared with $150\text{ rad/s}$), because the same torque gives a larger angular acceleration to the object with the smaller rotational inertia.
options.why: The angular acceleration is $\alpha=\tau/I$ with $I=0.0640\text{ kg m}^2$ for the solid sphere and $0.0800\text{ kg m}^2$ for the solid disk, so $\omega=\alpha t$ is larger for the solid sphere.

options.text: The solid disk is spinning faster, because it has the larger rotational inertia and so it stores more rotational energy.
options.why: Confuses a larger rotational inertia with a larger angular speed; the same torque gives it a smaller angular acceleration.

options.text: The solid sphere is spinning faster, because the torque acts for a longer time on it.
options.why: Invents a different time of action; the torque acts on both objects for the same time.

options.text: The two objects are spinning at the same speed, because they have the same mass, the same radius and the same torque.
options.why: Overlooks that the rotational inertia also depends on how the mass is distributed.

payload.stem: A solid sphere and a solid disk, each of mass $2\text{ kg}$ and radius $0.2\text{ m}$, are mounted on identical frictionless axles through their centers and start from rest. The same constant torque of $1\text{ N m}$ is applied to each for $6\text{ s}$. Which statement about the angular speeds after $6\text{ s}$ is correct and best justified?

options.text: The solid disk is spinning faster, because it has the larger rotational inertia and so it stores more rotational energy.
options.why: Confuses a larger rotational inertia with a larger angular speed; the same torque gives it a smaller angular acceleration.

options.text: The solid sphere is spinning faster, because the torque acts for a longer time on it.
options.why: Invents a different time of action; the torque acts on both objects for the same time.

options.text: The solid sphere is spinning faster ($187\text{ rad/s}$ compared with $150\text{ rad/s}$), because the same torque gives a larger angular acceleration to the object with the smaller rotational inertia.
options.why: The angular acceleration is $\alpha=\tau/I$ with $I=0.0320\text{ kg m}^2$ for the solid sphere and $0.0400\text{ kg m}^2$ for the solid disk, so $\omega=\alpha t$ is larger for the solid sphere.

options.text: The two objects are spinning at the same speed, because they have the same mass, the same radius and the same torque.
options.why: Overlooks that the rotational inertia also depends on how the mass is distributed.
